topic.subject: social
topic.title: The Mughal empire
topic.scope: Babur to Aurangzeb, mansabdari, jagirs, zabt revenue, sulh-i kul, Akbar Nama, relations with Rajputs

misconceptions.statement: The Mughal Empire was a single, unchanging entity from Babur to Aurangzeb.
misconceptions.why: Textbooks often present the empire as a monolithic block, ignoring the significant territorial and administrative shifts over 150 years.
misconceptions.fix: The empire grew and changed significantly; it started as a small kingdom under Babur and expanded into a vast subcontinental power under Akbar and Aurangzeb.

probe.question: Did the Mughal Empire cover the same amount of land during Babur's reign as it did under Aurangzeb?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because it was the same Mughal Empire throughout.

misconceptions.statement: Mughals were always the dominant power in India from the moment they arrived.
misconceptions.why: Students often conflate the eventual success of the empire with its initial arrival, ignoring the struggles against Lodi or Rajputs.
misconceptions.fix: Babur had to fight several battles, such as Panipat and Khanua, to establish his authority against existing local powers.

probe.question: Was Babur immediately accepted as the ruler of all India when he arrived?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, he was the Mughal emperor and everyone bowed to him.

misconceptions.statement: A jagir was a piece of land that the mansabdar owned permanently like a landlord.
misconceptions.why: Students confuse the Mughal administrative system with the later British Zamindari system or modern land ownership.
misconceptions.fix: A jagir was a right to collect revenue from a land area; the mansabdar did not own the land and was frequently transferred.

probe.question: Could a mansabdar pass his jagir to his son as an inheritance?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because it was his land.

misconceptions.statement: All mansabdars were military generals who only fought in wars.
misconceptions.why: The term 'mansab' is often simplified in classrooms to mean 'army rank' without explaining the civil administrative duties.
misconceptions.fix: Mansabdars held a rank that determined their status and salary, and they were responsible for both military and civil administrative tasks.

probe.question: What was the primary job of a mansabdar?
probe.wrong_answer: To lead soldiers in battle and nothing else.

concepts.name: Governance and Ideology: Zabt and Sulh-i Kul

misconceptions.statement: Sulh-i kul meant that the Mughal emperors gave up their own religion.
misconceptions.why: Students interpret 'universal peace' as a total abandonment of personal religious identity, which contradicts their understanding of religious loyalty.
misconceptions.fix: Sulh-i kul was a policy of tolerance where the emperor respected people of all faiths without forcing them to abandon their own beliefs.

probe.question: Did Akbar stop being a Muslim when he practiced sulh-i kul?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, he gave up his religion to be neutral.

misconceptions.statement: Zabt was a system where the government took all the crops from the farmers.
misconceptions.why: Students confuse the term 'revenue' with the physical seizure of all produce, failing to understand the concept of taxation.
misconceptions.fix: Zabt was a revenue system where the government calculated the tax based on the average produce and prices, usually paid in cash.

probe.question: What happened to the farmer's crops under the zabt system?
probe.wrong_answer: The government took all the grain to the palace.

requires_topics: Basic concepts of kingship and taxation
